entries.title: The substitution model
entries.summary: Applying a compound procedure = evaluating the body with the formal parameters replaced by the arguments; it is for thinking, not a description of the real interpreter; it breaks down with mutable data.

entries.title: Applicative order vs normal order
entries.summary: Applicative: evaluates the arguments and applies; normal: fully expands and then reduces (evaluates (+ 5 1) twice in the example). They give the same value when substitution holds; Lisp uses applicative.

entries.title: Lexical scoping and block structure
entries.summary: A free variable of an internal procedure takes its value from the enclosing procedure: lexical scoping; associated with the block structure of Algol 60.

entries.title: First-class procedures
entries.summary: First-class elements can be named, passed as arguments, returned and stored in data structures; Lisp gives procedures this status.

entries.title: Procedures as arguments (sum)
entries.summary: `sum` takes term, a, next, b; with it sum-cubes, sum-integers and pi-sum are defined.

entries.title: Procedures as returned values
entries.summary: `deriv` takes a procedure and returns another (approximate derivative); Newton's method via newton-transform.

entries.title: Data abstraction: rational numbers
entries.summary: Data abstraction isolates the use of compound data from its construction; interface = selectors and constructors (make-rat, numer, denom).

entries.title: Abstraction barriers
entries.summary: Barriers isolate levels of the system (add-rat → make-rat/numer/denom → pairs); confining the dependence on the representation makes maintenance and modification easier.

entries.title: What is data? (pairs as procedures)
entries.summary: Data = constructors + selectors + conditions; cons/car/cdr can be implemented with procedures only (dispatch); the style is called message passing.

entries.title: Closure property
entries.summary: A combination operation has the property if its results can be combined by the same operation (cons of pairs); it enables hierarchical structures. Note p.141: SICP does not use 'closure' in the implementation sense.

entries.title: Note on the word 'closure'
entries.summary: The term comes from abstract algebra; SICP warns that the Lisp community uses closure for another technique (procedures with free variables), a sense not used in the book.

entries.title: Sequences as conventional interfaces
entries.summary: Enumerate, filter, map and accumulate as stages of a signal flow; a conventional interface for data structures.

entries.title: Multiple representations (complex numbers)
entries.summary: Complex numbers in rectangular or polar form: addition/subtraction natural in rectangular, multiplication/division in polar; principle of least commitment.

entries.title: Tagged data and dispatch on type
entries.summary: Type tags and generic selectors with cond; weaknesses: changing the selectors for each new type and name collisions; a non-additive technique.

entries.title: Data-directed programming
entries.summary: Two-dimensional operation×type table; packages installed with put; apply-generic looks up the method; generic selectors do not change when a representation is added.

entries.title: Message passing
entries.summary: Decomposes the table into columns: 'intelligent' objects that dispatch on the operation name; a useful technique, to be taken up again in ch. 3.

entries.title: Coercion between types
entries.summary: Coercion table; apply-generic tries to coerce one argument to the other's type; one procedure per pair of types.

entries.title: Type tower and hierarchies
entries.summary: Integer ⊂ rational ⊂ real ⊂ complex; the raise procedure goes up one level; general hierarchies are not towers (multiple supertypes).

entries.title: The cost of assignment
entries.summary: With set! substitution no longer holds: a variable becomes a place; equality/identity get complicated; the imperative style brings pitfalls (order of assignments).

entries.title: Referential transparency
entries.summary: A language in which equals can be substituted for equals is referentially transparent; set! violates this.
verify: equals can be substituted for equals

entries.title: The environment model
entries.summary: Environment = sequence of frames (tables of bindings) with a pointer to the enclosing environment; procedure = code + environment; applying creates a new frame; define and set! act on the frame.
verify: environment is a sequence of frames

entries.title: Frames as a repository of local state
entries.summary: make-withdraw: E1 holds balance; (W1 50) creates a frame whose enclosing environment is E1; W2 has another environment and independent state.

entries.title: Concurrency: time is of the essence
entries.summary: Assignment forces us to admit time; processes sharing balance can interleave read/compute/write and lose money; criterion: same result as some sequential order.
verify: same as if they had run sequentially

entries.title: Serializers
entries.summary: Sets of procedures of which only one execution at a time is allowed; make-serializer, parallel-execute; exchanging between accounts requires exposing the serializer.

entries.title: Mutex and test-and-set!
entries.summary: Serializers use a mutex; test-and-set! must be atomic; the implementation depends on the system (time-slicing or hardware instructions).

entries.title: Deadlock
entries.summary: Two processes waiting for each other; way out: number the resources and acquire the lowest-numbered one first; harder cases may require sophisticated techniques.

entries.title: Streams, delay and force
entries.summary: cons-stream = cons a (delay b); delay = lambda with no arguments; force calls it; memo-proc stores the result.

entries.title: Infinite streams
entries.summary: integers-starting-from, no-sevens, sieve of Eratosthenes, implicit definition of ones/integers/fibs.

entries.title: Mutability and delayed evaluation
entries.summary: Mutability and delayed evaluation do not mix well; streams allow modularity without assignment (Monte Carlo).

entries.title: Metacircular evaluator: eval and apply
entries.summary: An evaluator written in the language it evaluates; eval does case analysis on the syntax; apply distinguishes primitives from compounds.

entries.title: Data as programs; universal machine
entries.summary: The evaluator is seen as a universal machine: it imitates other machines described as Lisp programs.

entries.title: Separating analysis and execution (analyze)
entries.summary: analyze takes only the expression and returns an execution procedure that takes the environment; the analysis happens once.

entries.title: Lazy evaluation and thunks
entries.summary: Delayed arguments become thunks (expression + environment); forced in primitives, predicates and operators; memoization with evaluated-thunk.

entries.title: The amb operator and search
entries.summary: amb chooses ambiguously; (amb) fails; require discards; systematic search with backtracking; choice points.

entries.title: The amb evaluator: success and failure continuations
entries.summary: Execution procedures take environment, succeed and fail; side effects are undone when backtracking.

entries.title: Stop-and-copy garbage collection
entries.summary: Memory split into two halves; copies useful objects to the free half; broken heart and forwarding address; it is a compactor and examines only the useful part.

entries.title: Tail recursion in the explicit-control evaluator
entries.summary: The tail-recursive evaluator runs sqrt-iter without growing space; the metacircular one does not specify it; ev-sequence restores continue before the last expression.

entries.title: Pike's rules and McIlroy's philosophy
entries.summary: McIlroy's philosophy and Pike's rules (measure before optimizing; data dominates; 'there is no Rule 6') precede the 17 rules.

entries.title: The list of the 17 rules
entries.summary: Numbered list of the 17 rules from Modularity to Extensibility, abstracted by the author.

entries.title: Rule of Modularity
entries.summary: Simple parts connected by clean interfaces; problems stay local and one part can be updated without breaking the whole.

entries.title: Rule of Clarity
entries.summary: Write for whoever will maintain it; trading a small performance gain for great obscurity is a bad deal.

entries.title: Rule of Composition
entries.summary: Programs should connect; filters of text streams; the text stream imposes encapsulation.

entries.title: Rule of Separation
entries.summary: Separate policy from mechanism and interfaces from engines; they change on different time scales.

entries.title: Rule of Simplicity
entries.summary: Design for simplicity; complexity only where unavoidable; 'technical machismo' and inflated requirements.

entries.title: Rule of Parsimony
entries.summary: A big program only when it is shown that nothing smaller will do.

entries.title: Rule of Transparency
entries.summary: Design for visibility; transparent = you can understand what it does; discoverable = exposes internal state.

entries.title: Rule of Robustness
entries.summary: Child of transparency and simplicity; avoid special cases; tolerate unusual inputs.

entries.title: Rule of Representation
entries.summary: Fold knowledge into data so the logic can be simple; conversion array vs switch; Pike's Rule 5.

entries.title: Rule of Least Surprise
entries.summary: Model the interface on conventions and analogous programs; respect Unix traditions.

entries.title: Rule of Silence
entries.summary: With nothing surprising to say, say nothing; predates video terminals; the user's attention is a scarce resource.

entries.title: Rule of Repair
entries.summary: Repair what you can; when failing, fail noisily and early; mentions Postel's prescription.

entries.title: Rule of Economy
entries.summary: Programmer time is expensive; conserve it in preference to machine time.

entries.title: Rule of Generation
entries.summary: Avoid hand-hacking; write programs that write programs; parser/lexer generators.

entries.title: Rule of Optimization
entries.summary: Prototype before polishing; premature optimization (Knuth, whom he attributes to Hoare); K&P: 90% of the functionality now.

entries.title: Rule of Diversity
entries.summary: Distrust 'one true way'; many languages and open systems.

entries.title: Rule of Extensibility
entries.summary: Leave room to grow; self-describing versioned formats; not a license for unnecessary features.

entries.title: The single lesson: KISS
entries.summary: The whole philosophy boils down to the KISS principle.

entries.title: Textuality: serialization, interoperability and transparency
entries.summary: File formats and protocols involve serializing structures; addresses lose meaning; endianness and 32/64 bits cause problems; themes: interoperability, transparency, extensibility, economy.

entries.title: Text vs binary
entries.summary: Complex binary formats should be avoided; compression over text; binary only with volume that matters; extensibility weighs against binary.
verify: lie down until the feeling passes

entries.title: Case study: the Unix password file
entries.summary: Text with one record per line and colon-separated fields; the ~8% gain of binary does not compensate for editability and the use of grep.

entries.title: Metaformats for data files
entries.summary: DSV, RFC 822, cookie-jar, record-jar, XML and INI; use an existing metaformat instead of an idiosyncratic format.

entries.title: Multiprogramming: cooperating processes
entries.summary: Split programs into cooperating processes; Unix makes processes cheap, offers IPC and encourages textual formats; bugs accumulate at the interfaces.

entries.title: Pipes, redirection and filters
entries.summary: Pipe invented by McIlroy; programs as filters read from standard input and write to standard output.

entries.title: Threads: threat or menace?
entries.summary: Threads are a performance hack; contention in shared space, no encapsulation, hard to debug and not very portable; last resort.

entries.title: Minilanguages
entries.summary: Small domain languages; fewer lines, fewer bugs; three paths (two good, one dangerous: extending feature by feature).

entries.title: Taxonomy of languages
entries.summary: From the data file to general-purpose interpreters: declarative (m4, make, yacc/lex, XSLT), domain-imperative (bc/dc) and general.

entries.title: Designing minilanguages
entries.summary: Keep it simple; prefer structured data; avoid accidentally Turing-complete languages; consider extending/embedding a scripting language.

entries.title: Profiling: 90% of the time in 10% of the code
entries.summary: As a rule of thumb, 90% of the execution time is spent in 10% of the code; profilers identify these hot spots (outside the Rule of Optimization).
verify: 90% of the execution time of your program

entries.title: Interface patterns: filter and cantrip
entries.summary: Filter: stdin → stdout; cantrip: no input or output, only invocation and a numeric exit status.

entries.title: Silence is Golden (ch. 11)
entries.summary: Programs that chatter do not compose; status messages on standard output get in the way; only real errors go to standard error.

entries.title: The map of the territory: phases
entries.summary: Scanning, parsing, static analysis (binding), IR, optimization, code generation, VM and runtime.

entries.title: Front end, back end and IR
entries.summary: IR as the interface between source and target languages; a shared IR reduces N×M compilers.

entries.title: Shortcuts: single pass, tree-walk, transpilers
entries.summary: Single-pass compilers, tree-walk interpreters (slow), transpilers.

entries.title: Just-in-time compilation
entries.summary: JIT compiles to native code at load time; the most sophisticated ones recompile hot spots.

entries.title: Compilers vs interpreters
entries.summary: Compiling and interpreting are not mutually exclusive; CPython is an interpreter and has a compiler.

entries.title: Lexemes and tokens
entries.summary: A lexeme is the smallest sequence with meaning; token = lexeme + type + literal + line.

entries.title: Context-free grammars
entries.summary: A grammar generates strings; terminals, nonterminals and productions; a BNF variant.

entries.title: Precedence and associativity
entries.summary: Lox precedence table (equality to unary); stratified grammar; avoid left recursion.

entries.title: Recursive descent
entries.summary: Top-down parser that translates rules into code; used by GCC, V8 and Roslyn.

entries.title: Error recovery: panic mode
entries.summary: On detecting an error the parser synchronizes by discarding tokens up to a statement boundary; avoids cascading errors.

entries.title: The expression problem
entries.summary: Types×operations table; OO makes new rows easy, ML new columns; neither makes both easy.

entries.title: The Visitor pattern
entries.summary: Approximates the functional style in OO: adds operations without touching the types; Visitor interface with one method per type; accept calls the right method.

entries.title: Static scope and the resolution rule
entries.summary: A used variable refers to the preceding declaration with the same name in the innermost scope; part of the static semantics.

entries.title: Dynamic scope (definition)
entries.summary: In dynamic scope you do not know what a name refers to until runtime; Lox has no dynamic variables, but methods and fields are dynamic.

entries.title: The scope bug with closures (showA)
entries.summary: showA prints 'global' and then 'block' without reassignment: the closure captures the mutable Environment; persistent environments or a resolver.

entries.title: The resolution pass (Resolver)
entries.summary: Static pass after the parser and before execution; stack of scopes; computes the distance (hops) per use; the interpreter uses getAt(distance).

entries.title: Resolution errors
entries.summary: A duplicate variable in a local scope and a top-level return are static errors; the interpreter does not run if there is an error.

entries.title: Why bytecode (tree-walk vs native)
entries.summary: jlox takes ~72 s for fib(40) against 0.5 s in C; the AST has many pointers and poor locality; native is fast but complex and not portable; bytecode sits in the middle.

entries.title: Chunks, constants and lines
entries.summary: Chunk = dynamic array of bytes + constant pool + parallel line array.

entries.title: The stack VM: ip, run and stackTop
entries.summary: ip points to the next instruction (a pointer is faster than an index); run() with a switch; stack with stackTop after the last element.

entries.title: Pratt parsing and single-pass compilation
entries.summary: Top-down operator precedence; ParseRule table (prefix, infix, precedence); parsePrecedence with a loop; emits bytecode directly.

entries.title: Global (late bound) and stack-local variables
entries.summary: Globals in a hash table, resolved late; locals on the VM stack, resolved at compile time.

entries.title: Calls and CallFrames
entries.summary: CallFrame = function, ip and slots; fixed array of frames in the VM; maximum depth FRAMES_MAX.

entries.title: Closures and upvalues
entries.summary: An upvalue is the indirection (from Lua) to a local of an enclosing function; each closure has an array of upvalues.

entries.title: Open and closed upvalues
entries.summary: Open points to the stack; closed keeps the value on the heap; OP_CLOSE_UPVALUE and closeUpvalues.

entries.title: Hash tables: tombstones
entries.summary: Deletion requires tombstones; open addressing with linear probing; interned strings.

entries.title: Why collect garbage; reachability and roots
entries.summary: A managed language gives the illusion of infinite memory; reachable = referenceable; roots reached directly by the VM.

entries.title: Mark-sweep in clox
entries.summary: Mark from the roots (stack, globals, CallFrames, open upvalues, compiler) and sweep the unmarked.

entries.title: Tricolor abstraction and the gray stack
entries.summary: White, gray (worklist) and black; grayStack managed outside the GC.

entries.title: Sweep and weak references (string pool)
entries.summary: sweep frees whites and clears marks; the string table is a weak reference: tableRemoveWhite between marking and sweep.

entries.title: When to collect: throughput and latency
entries.summary: Throughput vs latency; next GC threshold = bytes allocated × factor 2.

entries.title: GC bugs and generational collection
entries.summary: Objects held only on the C stack during allocation get swept; fix by pushing them on the stack; alternatives: reference counting, generational, Cheney (exercise).

entries.title: Profiler-guided optimization
entries.summary: The profiler showed tableGet at 72% of the time; replacing modulo with a bit mask reduced it to 35%; profilers also verify solutions.

entries.title: NaN boxing
entries.summary: A 16-byte Value drops to 8 using the 51 free bits of quiet NaNs; 48-bit pointers + 3 tag bits.

not_in_book.note: SICP and TAUP do not define dynamic scoping (v1 cited TAUP p.364). Only CI defines it (p.131, p.161). Label [extrapolation] or cite CI.
The term does not appear in any of the three books. SICP deals with 'data as programs' (p.352-354).
SICP describes stop-and-copy (p.489-494) without naming Cheney; CI cites Cheney in an exercise (p.533).
Copy-on-write does not appear in TAUP or in the other books of the package.
CI explains the Visitor without using 'double dispatch' (p.72-75).
CI does not relate the Visitor to the Open/Closed Principle.
TAUP (2003) does not mention JSON or YAML; it cites DSV, RFC 822, XML, INI (p.139-146).
SICP says analyze is 'significantly more efficient' (p.360), without 'orders of magnitude'.
CI does not give these multipliers; it gives 72 s (jlox) vs 0.5 s (C) for fib(40) (p.232).
CI does not state the year of Pratt's work.
TAUP does not prescribe --help/-v/-f as a POSIX/GNU convention; it only says to follow Unix traditions (p.45).
Chapter 9 (Control Flow) is not in the CI PDF (p.139→140).
SICP does not use 'closure' in the sense of an implementation technique (p.141, note 6).
